findings.title: k_circt truncates comb.concat to the parsed result width, silently dropping the high operands (disagrees with circt on 240/256 cases)
findings.detail: CombConcatRule.compute() packs the operands correctly (packed = (packed << width) | value), but it does not override SemanticRule.width(). SemanticRule.apply() (semantics.py:301) therefore truncates the packed value with SemanticRule.width() -> _result_width(op) (semantics.py:269 and 188), i.e. the *parsed result type*. For `comb.concat %a, %b : i4, i4` the parser assigns the result type i4, because Operation.result_types_from_trailing (mlir/ir.py:1076) returns trailing_types[-1] and circt.comb_dialect.ConcatOp (comb_dialect.py:338) does not override it the way ICmpOp (comb_dialect.py:297) and ParityOp (comb_dialect.py:487) do. The circt simulator does not depend on that result type: ConcatOp.evaluate computes `total = sum(widths)` from the operand types (comb_dialect.py:383) and is correct. Consequence: the two layers give different answers for every concat whose high operands carry a set bit -- 240/256 two-operand i4,i4 concats and 256/256 three-operand i1,i4,i4 concats. CombConcatRule is the only width-changing comb rule missing a width() override (compare CombICmpRule at semantics.py:608 and CombParityRule at semantics.py:690, both of which return 1). k_circt's own TypeResolver agrees with the bad result type (reports `M::r : i4`) while ConcatOp.infer_width() reports 8, so the stack is internally inconsistent as well. inputs/alu.mlir and inputs/counter.mlir contain no comb.concat, which is why the required 1024-combo ALU differential and the 300-cycle counter differential are both clean and the harness still passes.

findings.title: CircuitSimulator.reset_state() ignores constant-driven reset values: registers power on at 0 instead of their reset value, diverging from k_circt and from its own reset-edge behaviour
findings.detail: reset_state() builds `env = self._port_environment()`, which contains only input-port values -- no combinational settle has run, so no hw.constant result is in it. CompRegOp.reset_state(env) then calls declared_reset_value(env) -> read_operand(env, RESET_VALUE=3) (seq_dialect.py:232), misses the `%c9` operand and falls back to the attribute default 0. k_circt does this correctly: state.py:227 `_reset_value_of` walks to the defining op of operand 3 and reads its `value` attribute (its docstring even explains why: "the reset value has to be known before any rule has settled the design"). So the two layers disagree on the power-on state and on the entire output series from cycle 0 on. circt is also self-inconsistent: a reset *edge* does resolve the constant (CompRegOp.next_value -> declared_reset_value with the settled env, seq_dialect.py:251), so sim.step({'reset':1}) yields reg=9 while sim.reset() yields reg=0 -- directly contradicting the docstring on simulator.py:240, "Assert reset: every register returns to its reset value." inputs/counter.mlir uses reset value 0 (%c0_i8), which is exactly why the required 300-cycle and reset-asserted-then-released differentials are both clean; any non-zero reset value exposes it.

findings.title: record_configurations=True snapshots the configuration after the clock edge, so TraceEntry.configuration contradicts the TraceEntry it is attached to
findings.detail: `Kimulator.step` runs the whole cycle (`StatefulCircuit.step`, which ends by firing ClockEdgeRule) and only then takes `self.config.snapshot()`. The resulting `TraceEntry` therefore carries a configuration from the *next* cycle: `entry.configuration.cycle == entry.cycle + 1`, `entry.configuration.state` is the post-edge register state while `entry.state` is the pre-edge state, and `entry.configuration.next_state` is always empty because ClockEdgeRule (semantics.py, `config.next_state.clear()`) drains `<next>` before the snapshot — even though `entry.next_state` holds the staged values. The module docstring (kimulator.py:17-19) states a TraceEntry holds "the inputs, the register state before the edge, the settled outputs and the ordered list of RuleApplication records that produced them"; the attached configuration is not that state, so the one recorded K configuration per cycle is unusable for reconstructing the cycle it labels.

The repro's raw observations reproduce exactly (34 source lines -> 30 printed, not byte-identical, `func.return`), but the "EXPECTED per the comment: identical to source, 34 lines" is the auditor's own invention, not a requirement of this project, and the code's actual contract contradicts it.

1. 30 IS line-for-line. sample_arith.mlir is 34 lines = 30 statement lines + 2 blank lines + 2 `//` comment lines (verified by counting). The printer emits exactly one line per source statement line, so the comment at src/run_experiments.py:45-46 is a loose but substantively accurate paraphrase of a real 1:1 mapping.

2. The project's authoritative contract test encodes precisely this behaviour. /workspace/tests/test_outputs.py:161-172 (`test_printer_matches_source_statement_count`) filters blanks and `//` comments out of the source before comparing counts:

   self.assertEqual(len(source_lines), len(print_module(self.module).splitlines()))
Dropping comments/blank lines is therefore a deliberate, test-pinned design choice, not undocumented behaviour. src/mlir/parser.py:151 documents it at the tokenizer too: "Turns MLIR source text into a token list (`//` comments are dropped)."

4. `return` -> `func.return` is deliberate normalization of the func-dialect shorthand to its qualified name, and it parses back cleanly (tests/test_outputs.py:153-159 asserts round-trip stability AND the literal 30).

The claim that it "would mislead anyone adding a printer test" is directly contradicted by the fact that the printer tests already exist, already assert 30, and already spell out the comment/blank filtering. findings.title: comb.concat gets width 4 instead of 8: SUMMED_WIDTH_OPS inference never runs and the conflict check that would catch it is dead code (wrong simulation output)
findings.detail:
`_infer_once` skips any result whose seeded binding is already resolved (`if binding is not None and binding.is_resolved: continue`, types.py:416-417). Every result parsed from source is seeded as *declared* by `_seed_declared_types`, so (a) the `SUMMED_WIDTH_OPS` rule (types.py:297, 459-463) is never applied, and (b) the conflict branch at types.py:423-428 is statically unreachable — `previous` is always None when it is evaluated, so `TypeConflict` is never constructed and `is_consistent`/`is_complete` are unconditionally True.

findings.title: Symbol references are bound against a flat, scope-blind table, so a call resolves to a shadowed nested symbol instead of the visible one
findings.detail:

findings.detail: `CircuitState` is a `Dict[str, RegisterCell]` keyed by `register_key(op)` (state.py:104-106, populated from `from_module` at state.py:120-134), and `register_key` (src/k_circt/semantics.py:163-171) prefers the op's `reg_name` (i.e. the MLIR `name` attribute) over the *unique* SSA result name. In the 2-stage shift register below the k_circt output is stuck at 0 for all time while `src/circt/simulator.py` (which keeps `self._registers` as a list, simulator.py:188-190) gets it right. A duplicate `name` attribute is legal MLIR and CIRCT routinely attaches `name` to `seq.compreg`. But `_port_environment()` (simulator.py:273-287) contains only port names/block arguments - the `hw.constant` that drives the reset-value operand has not been evaluated - so `read_operand(env, RESET_VALUE)` silently falls back to 0 and every register powers on at 0 no matter what the IR declares. k_circt's `_reset_value_of` (src/k_circt/state.py:227-253) resolves the constant-like defining op directly and gets it right, so the two layers disagree. With `inputs/counter.mlir` the reset value is 0 and the disagreement is invisible, which is why the harness passes; with any non-zero reset constant the layers diverge on cycle 0, and for a design that never asserts reset (below) they diverge on every cycle forever. The simulator docstring at simulator.py:240 ("every register returns to its reset value") does not match what the code does.

findings.title: cf.cond_br whose two successors are the same block always passes the true-branch operands, ignoring the condition
findings.detail: `CFCondBranchRule.successor` splits the terminator's operand list into the true-args group and the false-args group, then chooses with `arguments[:split] if taken is true_dest else arguments[split:]`. The choice is made by *object identity* of the destination block rather than by the condition that was already computed on line 1066. When both successor positions name the same block - legal MLIR, and something canonicalization/lowering readily produces - `op.successors[0] is op.successors[1]`, so `taken is true_dest` is True even when the condition is false, and the block argument is bound from the true-branch operand group. The result is a wrong value with no diagnostic. This is on the `execute_function` multi-block path (state.py:495-526 -> semantics.py:1029-1044 -> `transfer` at semantics.py:1110-1118). Fix is to key off the condition, e.g. compute `use_true = bool(condition & 1)` once and select the slice with that.

findings.title: StatefulCircuit.output(name) raises "'res' is not an output port of this module" for a port that IS an output port
findings.detail: `StatefulCircuit.output` (state.py:459-465, surfaced as `Kimulator.output`) validates the requested name against `self.config.outputs` - the *cached result of the last settle* - not against `self._output_ports`. Before the first `settle()`/`evaluate()`/`step()`, and after any `reset()` (which calls `config.reset()` at state.py:364 and so empties the `<outputs>` cell), `config.outputs` is `{}`, so any named lookup raises `SemanticError: "'res' is not an output port of this module"` even though `kim.output_names == ['res']`. The message is factually wrong, and the behaviour is inconsistent three ways: `output()` with no name returns the `default` (0) instead of raising, `Kimulator.reset()` turns a working `output('res')` back into an exception, and the equivalent circt call `CircuitSimulator.get_output('res')` (simulator.py:366-374) returns 0. The check should be against the module's output port names, with `default` returned for a port that has not been settled yet.

findings.title: RegisterCell's documented two-phase API (stage/commit/next_value/cycles_latched) is never used by the cycle driver, so cycles_latched is permanently 0
findings.detail: `RegisterCell` advertises a "-- two-phase update --" block (state.py:71-94) with `stage()`, `commit()`, `next_value` and a `cycles_latched` counter, and `CircuitState` mirrors it with `stage()`/`commit()` (state.py:150-157). `StatefulCircuit.step` (state.py:416-435) bypasses all of it: the staged values go into the configuration's `<next>` cell via `SeqRegisterLatchRule`, `ClockEdgeRule` commits `<state>`, and the cells are then refreshed with `CircuitState.sync_from` -> `RegisterCell.write` (state.py:184-188, 144-148), which does not touch `next_value` or `cycles_latched`. Consequently, on a live simulation `cell.next_value` is always `None` and `cell.cycles_latched` is always 0, while the equivalent circt counter `SeqOp.cycles_ticked` (src/circt/seq_dialect.py:131-134) correctly reports the number of latches. `grep -rn 'cycles_latched|\.stage\(|\.commit\(\)' src` confirms nothing in `src/` ever calls them - the only callers are unit tests that poke a bare `RegisterCell`. Either the driver should route through `CircuitState.stage()`/`commit()` or these members should not be presented as the register's update mechanism, because they report state that is never true after a real cycle.

No requirement ties the k_circt cell counter to circt's SeqOp.cycles_ticked, and the two layers have deliberately different state architectures: circt's simulator mutates op objects (simulator.py:398 register.commit(value), which is why its counter increments), while k_circt keeps state in configuration cells rewritten by semantic rules. The APIs are not even parallel — circt.SeqOp.next_value is a method taking an env (seq_dialect.py:126) whereas RegisterCell.next_value is a plain field.

(4) The API is not broken. Driven directly it is correct and self-consistent, and agent_tests/test_k_circt.py:306-309 exercises and asserts it (passes). cycles_latched == 0 is truthful: it counts commit() calls, and zero occurred because the driver latches through the <next>/<state> cells.

(5) Both suites are green: tests/test_outputs.py 25/25 OK, pytest agent_tests/ 76 passed.

What is left is that RegisterCell.stage/commit and CircuitState.stage/commit (state.py:150-157) are unused by the driver — dead helper code with a mild trap (a cell-level stage() is invisible to step() because load_into only copies snapshot(), state.py:178-182). result.reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not. The repro reproduces exactly, the mechanism is confirmed by reading the code, and the "expected" behaviour is the project's own documented intent rather than the auditor's invention.

Mechanism (all verified by reading): src/circt/simulator.py:243-250 loops over registers, builds `env = self._port_environment()` and calls `register.reset_state(env)`. That env exists for exactly one reason — to resolve the reset-value operand — but `_port_environment` (src/circt/simulator.py:272-287) only inserts block arguments and port names; results of `hw.constant` are never evaluated into it. `CompRegOp.declared_reset_value` (src/circt/seq_dialect.py:232-236) then calls `read_operand(env, RESET_VALUE)`, and `read_operand` (src/circt/hw_dialect.py:352-367) silently returns `default=0` on a miss. `step()` is unaffected because `settle()` (src/circt/simulator.py:290-322) folds the constants into env before `next_value` runs.

The finding is stronger than the cross-layer framing suggests: circt is self-inconsistent. For one register with `hw.constant 200` as reset value, `sim.step({"rst":1})` yields reg=200, `sim.reset_state()` yields reg=0, and a builder-constructed `CompRegOp(reset_value=200).reset_state({})` yields 200. So the docstring at src/circt/simulator.py:240 ("Assert reset: every register returns to its reset value") is falsified without any reference to k_circt — the same simulator gives two different answers for "assert reset" depending on entry point, and the parsed-IR path disagrees with the builder path for equivalent designs.

The expected value is not invented. src/k_circt/state.py:227-233 documents precisely this hazard ("the constant behind that operand is read directly - the reset value has to be known before any rule has settled the design"), and src/circt/seq_dialect.py:123 calls reset_state "Return the element to its power-on / reset state." Nothing in either layer models an undefined/X power-on as a deliberate design choice; the code actively tries to read the declared value and fails silently.

It is latent only because inputs/counter.mlir:6 uses `reset %reset, %c0_i8` (value 0), so the fallback is indistinguishable from the correct answer. `python3 tests/test_outputs.py` (25 tests) and `pytest agent_tests/` (81 tests) both pass, including agent_tests/test_circt.py:187-189 which does exercise `sim.reset_state()` but only on the zero-reset counter. `reset_state()` is also called from `CircuitSimulator.__init__` (src/circt/simulator.py:202), so every simulator's power-on state goes through the broken path.

One correction to the report: the divergence is confined to power-on state. Once reset is actually asserted, the layers reconverge (both produce [200, 201, 202] afterwards). The "diverge forever" case is real but requires a design that never asserts reset, as in the Swap repro. Medium severity is right: wrong results for any non-zero reset constant, plus a docstring that lies.

I then confirmed circt is self-inconsistent independent of k_circt, on module @One with `%c200 = hw.constant 200 : i8` as the compreg reset value:

findings.title: k_circt derives every result width from the parsed result type and never uses the dialect's infer_width(), so comb.concat with forward-referenced operands evaluates differently than the CIRCT simulator (2 vs 42)
findings.detail:
`_result_width()` (src/k_circt/semantics.py:188) is the only width source for `SemanticRule.truncate`, and it looks *only* at `bit_width_of(result.type)`. The circt layer, by contrast, evaluates `comb.concat` from `ConcatOp.infer_width()` = sum of operand widths (src/circt/comb_dialect.py:376-393). `infer_width` is never called anywhere in src/k_circt (grep: zero hits), so the two layers use different width rules despite the package docstring at src/k_circt/__init__.py:15-17 ("the hardware dialects, port model and bit-width rules come from src.circt") and the comb docstring at src/circt/comb_dialect.py:5 ("the simulator, the folder and the K-CIRCT semantic rules all share one definition of what each gate means").

The recent fix in `ConcatOp.build_parsed` (comb_dialect.py:361-371) patches the stale result type at parse time, but only when the operand types are already known at build time. A hw body is a graph region (see src/circt/simulator.py:9-16; inputs/counter.mlir itself uses a forward reference), so when a concat operand is defined *later* in the block, `infer_width()` returns 0 at build time and the result type stays at the parser's default (trailing_types[-1], i.e. the last *operand* type). After parsing, `op.infer_width()` == 6 while `op.result(0).type` == i2, and the Kimulator masks the correct 42 down to 2.

Same root cause shows up twice more: (a) k_circt's own type layer reports `T::r : i2` width 2 with `conflicts == []` and `is_complete == True`, even though `SUMMED_WIDTH_OPS` (src/k_circt/types.py:297,459) knows concat sums operand widths -- the summing rule is only reached for *unresolved* bindings, so a wrong-but-present type is never re-checked; (b) the printer emits `hw.output %r : i2` inside a module declared `out o: i6`.

cd /workspace && python3 -c "
import sys; sys.path.insert(0,'src')
import circt, k_circt
from mlir.parser import parse
src='hw.module @T(in %a: i4, in %b: i2, out o: i6) {\n  %r = comb.concat %x, %y : i4, i2\n  %x = comb.add %a, %a : i4\n  %y = comb.add %b, %b : i2\n  hw.output %r : i6\n}\n'
print('circt:', circt.CircuitSimulator(circt.find_module(parse(src),'T')).evaluate({'a':5,'b':3}))
print('k_circt:', k_circt.Kimulator(parse(src),'T').evaluate({'a':5,'b':3}))"

Actual:
  circt:   {'o': 42}
  k_circt: {'o': 2}
Expected: both 42 (x=10 on i4, y=2 on i2 -> concat = 10<<2 | 2 = 42; op.infer_width() == 6 for this op while op.result(0).type == i2).
With the operands written *before* the concat the same file gives 42 in both layers, so the divergence is purely parse-order dependent.

findings.title: CircuitSimulator never applies a register's declared reset-value operand at power-on (port-only env), so cycle 0 disagrees with the Kimulator (0 vs 7)
findings.detail:
`CircuitSimulator.reset_state()` (src/circt/simulator.py:239-253) is documented as "Assert reset: every register returns to its reset value" and calls `register.reset_state(env)` with `env = self._port_environment()`. That env contains only block arguments / input ports -- never the `hw.constant` that supplies the reset value -- so `CompRegOp.declared_reset_value(env)` (src/circt/seq_dialect.py:233-237) reads the missing operand and falls back to 0. A register with a non-zero reset constant therefore powers on at 0 in the circt layer.

The k_circt layer does resolve it: `_reset_value_of()` (src/k_circt/state.py:227-256) walks the reset-value operand back to its constant-like defining op and reads the attribute, seeding `RegisterCell.reset_value`. The result is that the same IR gives different cycle-0 register state and different cycle-0 outputs from the two layers, for both `seq.compreg` and `seq.firreg`. inputs/counter.mlir hides this because its reset constant is 0.

findings.title: Printer re-labels a terminator's leading operand as a successor argument, silently dropping the cf.cond_br condition from the printed IR
findings.detail: `Printer._successor_arguments()` (src/mlir/printer.py:299-317) recovers successor argument groups by taking the *last* `sum(block.num_arguments)` operands of a terminator, and `_format_op` (printer.py:262-268) then removes exactly those from the operand list. When a successor block declares more arguments than the terminator actually supplies, the slice eats the leading operands instead: `cf.cond_br %c, ^bb1, ^bb2` with `^bb1(%x: i32)` prints as `cf.cond_br ^bb1(%c : i1), ^bb2` -- the condition is gone and `%c` has been re-purposed as bb1's argument, i.e. the printed text parses cleanly but denotes a different program. `ModuleOp.verify()` returns `[]` both for the input and for the re-parsed output, so nothing flags it, and the round-trip stability check still reports "stable" because the corruption is idempotent. The printer's contract ("a faithful inverse of the parser", echoed in src/run_experiments.py:45-47) does not hold here.

from mlir.parser import parse
from mlir.printer import print_module
src='module {\n  func.func @f(%arg0: i32) -> i32 {\n    %c = arith.cmpi sgt, %arg0, %arg0 : i32\n    cf.cond_br %c, ^bb1, ^bb2\n  ^bb1(%x: i32):\n    return %x : i32\n  ^bb2:\n    return %arg0 : i32\n  }\n}\n'
m=parse(src); print('verify:', m.verify()); print([l for l in print_module(m).splitlines() if 'cond_br' in l])"

Actual:

Expected: the condition operand must survive printing (e.g. `cf.cond_br %c, ^bb1, ^bb2`), or verify() should reject a branch that does not supply its successor's block arguments.

findings.title: Kimulator advertises sv.module / firrtl.module bodies and reuses circt's hw dialect, but the rule set covers none of hw's data ops or any sv op, so circuits the circt simulator evaluates fail with SemanticError
findings.detail:
`circuit_rules()` (src/k_circt/semantics.py:1232-1280) registers rules for hw.constant / hw.wire / hw.output, all 19 comb ops and the seq registers, but nothing for the remaining evaluable hw ops. Comparing registered dialect classes that implement `evaluate()` against `CIRCUIT_RULES.handles(name)` gives: hw -> ['hw.array_create','hw.array_get','hw.bitcast','hw.instance','hw.struct_create','hw.struct_extract'], seq -> ['seq.hlmem'], sv -> all 9 ops, fsm -> 3 ops, firrtl -> 6 ops (comb / arith / cf / func are fully covered).

This is not merely unimplemented surface: `hw.bitcast` parses, the circt simulator evaluates it, and the Kimulator raises `SemanticError: no combinational rule for operation 'hw.bitcast'`. Worse, `MODULE_OPS` (src/k_circt/state.py:44) lists 'sv.module' and 'firrtl.module', so `find_hw_module`/`StatefulCircuit` accept an sv.module and build its port lists, then die on the first body op (`sv.wire`). The advertised entry points therefore accept module kinds the rule set cannot execute.
